- When sentiment is consistently bullish (high sentiment levels) and news volume is high, model tends to overestimate prices — apply downward bias correction.
- After sharp price spikes, model often overshoots and fails to correct — reduce forecast by 5–10% in next period if sentiment turns neutral or negative.
- If sentiment shows strong downward momentum (negative sentiment change) and price is rising, model may lag — adjust forecast downward by 2–5% to align with sentiment shift.
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed, model overfits recent trends — use moving average of last 5–7 days to smooth forecast.
- If true outcome is consistently below model (especially in early periods), model may be overconfident — reduce forecast by 3–7% for next period if sentiment remains neutral or weak.
- In high-news-volume periods, model often overreacts — apply a “news dampening” rule: reduce forecast by 1–3% for each additional news unit beyond 3.
- If sentiment is bullish but price is trending downward, model may misread sentiment — check for sentiment reversal and adjust forecast downward if sentiment change is negative.
- Model tends to underestimate price in low-news periods — increase forecast by 1–3% if news volume is low and sentiment is neutral or slightly bullish.
- When sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, model may overestimate — reduce forecast by 2–5% to reflect sentiment mismatch.
- In multi-week trends, model often fails to capture mean reversion — if price deviates >10% from 30-day moving average, adjust forecast toward average.
